child_eye_answers.q1: yes — The big circular place and draggable-looking map make me want to poke and move it.
child_eye_answers.q2: yes — The roads, river, and paths visibly continue beyond the screen, so I expect hidden places there.
child_eye_answers.q3: yes — It feels like one physical region, although the current empty terrain makes it feel unfinished.
child_eye_answers.q4: yes — Finding another place by traveling across the same landscape feels like continuing an adventure.
child_eye_answers.q5: yes — Free movement and uncertain off-screen space feel more game-like than choosing from a lesson menu.

strengths: The continuous geography makes traveling itself meaningful.
Off-screen paths and terrain create strong natural curiosity.
A production-quality unified illustration could feel like a memorable game world rather than navigation UI.
Locations have spatial relationships and can become familiar landmarks.
weaknesses: A production-quality continuous illustration would be extremely expensive and difficult to extend consistently.
Ten times more locations would produce a very large, increasingly cumbersome canvas.
Mobile users can become lost or miss locations without navigation assistance.
Incremental art additions risk reintroducing mismatched scale, lighting, and camera angle.
The current placeholder version is sparse enough that some children may not realize it can be panned.

child_eye_answers.q1: yes — The visible picture pins look tappable, and their motion should attract attention.
child_eye_answers.q2: no — Because nearly every destination is already visible, the edges promise little mystery.
child_eye_answers.q3: no — The equal-sized choices connected to a center read more like a visual level-selection menu than a continuous world.
child_eye_answers.q4: yes — Returning to an overview full of clearly different places makes choosing another destination easy.
child_eye_answers.q5: yes — The full-screen location art feels playful, but the overview still resembles an educational choice screen.

strengths: Each profession or place can retain its distinct, approved full-quality illustration.
The overview-to-focus interaction is immediately understandable on mobile.
New locations can be added incrementally without forcing their detailed illustrations into one camera system.
The architecture supports many realistically different places without visible scale mismatch.
Children can quickly understand their available choices and move between them.
weaknesses: Showing nearly everything at once weakens exploration and off-screen curiosity.
The overview behaves structurally like a destination menu.
Focusing a location removes the surrounding geography, weakening the feeling of physically arriving somewhere.
Equal circular pins make distinct places feel temporarily interchangeable.
With ten times more locations, the overview will require grouping, paging, or denser navigation and may become visibly menu-like.

recommendation_reasoning: Prototype A is the stronger architecture for the stated highest-priority qualities: game desire, discovery curiosity, and world feel. Its continuous geography makes movement, distance, and the unseen edge intrinsically interesting, whereas Prototype C solves production and scalability problems by turning the world into a highly usable atlas-style selector. Choose A only with explicit acceptance of its very high long-term art cost and expansion constraints; if production feasibility is the overriding constraint, C is the safer implementation.
requires_human_product_decision: Whether world feel and exploratory desire justify commissioning and maintaining one expensive continuous illustration.
Whether the product must support roughly tenfold location growth without periodically rebuilding the map artwork.
Whether mobile discoverability may rely on children learning free panning or requires explicit navigation assistance.
Whether preserving each location's independently approved art is more important than presenting all locations as parts of one physically coherent world.
